parsed.input_summary: Learner asks how many ATP glycolysis nets and how pyruvate reaches the mitochondrion.

render.title: Glycolysis yield and mitochondrial input
render.body:
Glycolysis breaks one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules in the cytoplasm. The net ATP gain is 2 molecules of ATP (the cell spends 2 ATP to start the process but recovers 4, so the net is 2). It also produces 2 NADH, which will later donate electrons to the electron transport chain.

Pyruvate does not simply diffuse into the mitochondrion. It crosses the outer mitochondrial membrane easily through pores called porins, but the inner membrane is tightly sealed. A dedicated protein complex called the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC) sits in the inner membrane and actively transports pyruvate into the matrix. Inside the matrix, an enzyme complex called pyruvate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA (releasing one molecule of CO2 per pyruvate in the process) and produces one more NADH. Acetyl-CoA then enters the Krebs cycle to continue energy extraction.
